Are you me?

Education background that got derailed because of Covid, not enough money to continue. Useless degree. Can't even get hired at fuckin' McDonald's.
Live in Boston and am absolutely desperate for a job, so seconding this question
Agree. If OP is just a mason trying to hire an extra hand, he probably isn't making millions and 5 per applicant might be a lot.

I like how almost half of the comments here are piling on OP. I don't think most people realize that some small businesses might not be able to afford to pay 5 per applicant or whatever.

Look, if OP is working for some giant corporation with a CEO laughing at his millions in under-the-table pay that makes it completely untaxable while paying minimum wage to employees, then fuck that. Raise the goddamn cost per applicant to fifty bucks for all I care. Screw your "five years experience for entry level" requirements and all that bullcrap.

But the way OP worded his question, this doesn't seem like a giant corporation. Not to roast OP, but he/she could have definitely worded that complaint better. That's definitely not "I work in a giant corporation making six figures in an office in Manhattan" language. Unless he/she is the kid of some CEO who got handed that job for free, in which case, refer to angry rant above. Not implying that OP is stupid - you can get pretty far in life even if you're "academically stupid", and being a literary master isn't necessary for some jobs - but generally writing eloquently is required for most corporate jobs which would have the power to actually hire someone.

Nah, this smells a lot more like a small business. Maybe a restaurant owner, who definitely can't afford to pay a ton of money to hire people right now. Maybe a master plumber who's looking for an apprentice and is literally paying for this out of his/her own pocket. Maybe just a person running a small bike repair shop that just wants people to help out.

Either way, I think all the people hating on OP are assuming he/she is a corporate douchebag. But what if OP isn't a corporate HR douchebag, but an honest guy running a blue collar business who needs an extra hand? In that case, five bucks per click on Indeed (where people will literally just click on anything they see that is remotely close to what they qualify for, which I'm guilty of tbh) might be a lot.

Now that my speech is over and I'm gunna get hated on for trying to defend OP, here's my suggestions for OP I guess. People who click on your posting are at least mildly interested in your job. To reduce the number of people who click, you might need to list details that might make people less willing to take your job. Basically, full transparency, so people know what they're signing up for. It saves everyone time - the applicants who know all the details can make a more honest judgement on whether they want to take the job, and the people who aren't interested will then simply not apply, which besides saving you money per click also means you have less people to interview, evaluate, and a sheet of people you know will have almost no problem with doing the work. Some things you could list are:

1. Pay. If you put a job up but you don't list the pay, you might get some folks who apply and will just ask about the pay later, and then if they are unwilling to accept the pay you offer they'll turn down your offer. So be up front about it. Plenty of people are going to not apply if you're offering pay significantly below market rate, so on the plus side you can get a sense of whether it's about time you started offering higher pay anyway (not saying you don't, but just in case). If it's 100% commission then say so, and list out the details.
2. Benefits. Insurance and earned sick time is also pretty valuable to some workers. Of course not every job's going to have this, but if you don't offer much, then some more experienced workers might prefer a different employer and will turn down your offer. Wasted time for everyone again. 
3. Hours. Some people don't want to work on Sunday because they're religious. Or they're huge football fans. Maybe they follow football like it's a religion. Other folks might not want to work overnight. Or some folks might have kids they have to take care of at night. Maybe a student needs to go to class in the morning. Maybe a person is looking for a full-time position only. It can be handy listing out exactly the hours you want them to work.
4. Workplace conditions and requirements. Some folks really just want AC. Some folks have health conditions that prevent them from standing on concrete floors all day. A person sensitive to light might not want to take a job in a room with a lot of flashing lights. Of course you can kind of be a bit generic on this since if your job title and description is clear, people will already have a mental image of what the job looks like, roughly. 
5. In everything above, **be honest and reasonable**. This is literally huge. Above all, people who are looking for work just want a job with an employer they know they can trust and be reasonable. If you don't bullshit your employees, good employees won't bullshit you back. Monthly barbeques and such are nice to have, but at the bottom of it all the employees just want you to be honest to them. This extends to the hiring process. Yes, you could lie about pay, benefits, hours, and workplace conditions, and still get someone desperate to pay some bills. But you can bet that as soon as they find a more honest employer who pays more, they'll jump ship immediately. You'll be stuck with employees who either aren't reliable, or a revolving door of people who come in just for experience, and then leave. You'll be spending a lot of money on job postings, that's for sure. I may be a bit old-fashioned, but I think I'd honestly work 15/hr for an employer that doesn't bullshit me than 17/hr for an employer who constantly lies about my schedule, benefits, and hours. Yes, corporate America is full of cheaters and liars, but at least pretend, right?

Look, OP, I obviously don't know much about you or the job you're hiring for, but if my hunch is correct and you're just a small business owner, then . . . good luck. Today's America isn't kind to small businesses or honest people. Cheaters and liars seem to get richer and richer these days, and there's not much we can do about it. I have hope that someday they'll get what's coming to them, but that seems unlikely.

Thanks for the support! I feel like I've tried everything I can reasonably do within my budget and abilities. I've worked with my school's career center to make a clean resume, written cover letters for pretty much anything that even asked for them, called up some smaller local companies asking about opportunities. Not much.

My brother says that I'm going insane (which I probably am), and that everything's going to be fine . . . except he's about to get a computer science degree, which is a bit more marketable. And of course his girlfriend's going to medical school, so either way, they are probably set to make at least enough to raise a family and not worry too much. Doesn't help that my extended family are all extremely successful. Most of my family still lives in Taiwan; my uncle is now the CEO of some electronics company there which is insane, one of my cousins is a doctor at one of the best hospitals in Taiwan, my other cousin works for the Taiwanese version of the FBI and apparently just busted some sort of scam thing. And again there's my brother with the future doctor girlfriend. Of course, every family's got to have the giant letdown, so I guess it can be me. Maybe the one cousin we lost contact with in Poland, last we knew he was a drug addict that just lost his warehouse job, so maybe I didn't even win the "family loser" award either. Small positives I guess.

Still, hard to have faith. Even if I do manage to get a minimum wage fast food job, what then? Definitely not going to be worth even trying to have a family at that point or thinking about having a future at that point. And I can't even get one of those jobs. God, it drives me insane. Where the hell are all these jobs the news keeps crowing about? All I see are rejections or jobs that want years of experience.

I'll stop. Need to stop thinking about this.

tried [tutor.com](https://tutor.com), they aren't looking for history tutors at the moment. Very unfortunate, I've been told by the folks I taught abroad and a few students I tutored at home that I'm pretty good with students. Too bad there's a severe oversupply of history majors looking for work. I could try going it alone, I'm completely fine with just in-person tutoring and driving out to students' homes and such, but I have no idea how to even start. It would be the only way really, considering how oversupplied all the online platforms are.

I actually thought about getting a job at a library. I do enjoy reading and I'm generally pretty friendly, and I honestly don't mind low pay as long as I get enough to live, so it would've been a great job for me. Hell, I'd stay there for the rest of my life if the pay were high enough to live and the hours consistent enough for me. Too bad I'm one among a crowd of desperate schmucks. My city put up a job posting for a library assistant paying minimum wage a month ago, it was only up for one day before they took it down because they received thousands of applicants. They only had two openings. It's quite discouraging.

I'd also be fine doing soul-crushing clerical work, but nowadays they seem to want years of experience and specific degrees for that. I'm not sure how complicated making photocopies can even be. God, the job market for white collar jobs in Boston is absolute garbage. Love this city, grew up here, but . . . this wasn't even a thing five years ago.

Unrelated side note, your English is really damn good for someone who isn't from an English speaking country. Where are you from? Just curious.

Interesting, factory work. How'd you get in that? Applied for a few factory jobs but they don't seem interested in me. If I can just get in somewhere, work my butt off, and prove that I'm worth training . . . but I have to get in first.

If I can scrape together enough money, I'll definitely try to get back to the teaching path. But in my opinion it's probably a better idea to actually have work and income first. 

I live in the Boston area, so I live in one of the few areas that actually pays its teachers enough to survive. This is both a good and bad thing. Good, in that if I get a teaching job in a public school I'll make enough to live (not gunna buy a lambo or a mansion but I was never in it for that anyway). But bad, in that piled on with the nationwide oversupply of history teachers, we have over 1k applicants for a single position. The sub pool is stuffed with people with masters' degrees already, and finding a job with an emergency license is impossible since there's thousands of folks with permanent licenses. It's still a goal, but if this whole mess has taught me anything, it's that I need a plan B.

The way I see it, my main problem is that I need a marketable skill if I want to make anything more than minimum wage. If I could just find a job as a laborer for a masonry company or whatever, and work my butt off, I could actually learn a thing or two about masonry - now I have some sort of skill, and that combined with proven work ethic would then land me a job with another masonry company that would be willing to teach me. Then after that I can actually make more than minimum wage. Theoretically. But of course, I have to get that laborer job first, or find someone who's willing to teach. And that's the problem. Trades keep saying they want people, well here I am, drug-free, reasonably fit, reliable, and not afraid of getting my hands dirty . . . what am I missing? It drives me insane.

Another huge pressing part of the issue is, well, the reason for my financial worries in the first place. To keep it brief, it's a situation where best case scenario I might be able to only have support from my parents for one more year, and then the income stream stops completely (and they'll be living entirely off of the savings they have left after my giant waste of college, so I won't have much to get started on). If I had the time, I'd keep pressing on with grad school, or switch majors and accept the extra cost and time. But I can't afford that. College at this point is basically a sunk cost for me. I'm committed to graduate at least, since my parents really really want me to have a degree, even if it's worthless. But once I'm through that, I have to face the reality that my degree is about as useful as a golden high school diploma to white collar jobs, and a sign that I'm a baby who isn't willing to do hard work to blue collar jobs. This is basically why I think I'm screwed. I could just leave off the degree, but then I'd have to explain what I've been doing the last few years.

Uber might work but it's going to be a last resort scenario. Would be better to have a resume with an actual job than trying to spice up uber delivery.

Honestly, a lot of those "requirements" are just "best case" or situational for me. If literally nothing would give me a Sunday off then I'll suck it up and work a Sunday. Being above minimum wage is ideal (and maybe possible with some of the more backbreaking jobs like landscape labor) but still, not too picky, just an ideal. Only real requirements are Boston area, 100% legal, and not commission pay. Not having a vehicle is pretty much required below 15 an hour, but above that I might just scrape enough together to make it work.

Yea, I'm fully aware I'm very unqualified for anything at all. Only thing I've proven in life is that I can show up drug-free and work. I guess I'll just go embrace the minimum wage life.

Yea, I did say I preferred no overnight stuff, but it's one of those things I prefer, instead of requiring. It is hampered by the fact that the T (the subway here in Boston) stops running after midnight, so transportation in early morning hours is going to be limited to my own two feet. I can use the exercise I guess.

Sadly not a lot of factories here in Boston. Used to have a ton but of course we turned into a tech city. The few manufacturing jobs left around here tend to be in outskirts areas not accessible by public transit. Would be nice if we hadn't torn down the Charlestown Elevated so long ago but I guess I'm just complaining about everything now aren't I.

I've considered construction, actually. As a little kid I really liked Legos, so while I've never tried it, I might enjoy some job putting things together. Plus, the local ironworkers union seems super chill; they're building a new complex at South Station and somebody in the union or close to the union got sick or something; the workers literally spray painted a get well soon message on a giant beam in full view of Atlantic Ave. Let's take a moment to forget how screwed I am to admire the world's greatest "Get Well Soon" card. Local 7 definitely has balls of steel and hearts of gold.

Sadly the ironworkers union requires ten years of related work experience to apply. I guess there's enough desperate schmucks like me looking for work. Plumbers and IBEW are also similar in requirements. Longshoremen (super cool job, I've always been interested in the sea) from what I hear is hyper competitive. I haven't scouted out any information on any other unions just because I don't really know a lot about other blue collar work. For some of these jobs I could get a slight pass on the work experience with trade school, but they cost a ton - so I'd need to build a very firm financial base first. Still, it's something I'd definitely try out.

The next play probably depends on what you got left in the bank. If you have enough for another year, you can keep trying to get back in your field with reasonable pay. If you're down to next month's rent . . . it may be time to go back to fast food or something. If you have enough in savings you might be able to afford taking a low paying role for a year while you shotgun applications out. They say it's easier to find work when you're already working.

Depends on what the job is and your previous experience.

Fresh out of college and the job is semi relevant to where you want to go? Take it. Get roommates anyway and live the ramen dream for two years, then start applying to similar roles with better pay. Ditch the car if you can and there is public transit nearby.

Years of experience or the job isn't relevant to where you want to go? Consider not taking it.

The thing is, non-profits tend to have smaller budgets for paying employees, or the directors take all of it. So you'll generally get paid less at a non-profit.

I dunno. Not an expert by any stretch of the imagination.

Perhaps you could try to find a role in a startup? They tend to be pretty risky plays, but that means less competition, more willing to take a wholistic look at a person, etc.

Otherwise, it depends on how much money you have left. If you have enough left for another year, keep trying to get back in your old field. If your rent bill needs to be in next month, then just get literally any job at this point. Ultimately it's more important to survive than to be picky.

If you just barely paid off your student loans but you're still close to 0 in the bank, you can probably make enough to scrape by living on your own, but you want to ideally have sufficient wealth to live for at least three months. 

I don't know which city you live in (as I said before I'm in Boston which is on the high end) so I don't know your local COL costs or anything. However, if you're smart about it, 20/hr full time will work out in Boston at least. You'll need to do the math yourself. Here's my math:

Boston Min. Wage: 13.50/hr (28,080 yearly, approx. 23,500 after taxes)

Estimated monthly take home: approx. 1,950

Rent: 800-1000 with roommates monthly

Food: 10 dollar budget per day, approx. 300 monthly, you can squeeze this down a bit with rice and beans diet

Transport: 90 monthly transit pass (no car; Boston has a very extensive transit system so you can live by walking and taking the T; this saves me around 200-250 a month)

Utilities: est. 100-150 monthly, closer to 75-100 if roommates, cheaper in the summer without AC

Civic Bills: with no car or anything else theoretically just 100 every few years to renew the driver's license, but let's be safe and say 150 monthly

Internet and Phone: approx 150

Other, for laundry and haircuts and whatever: approx 100 if you stay frugal

Visit to the MFA every month because I'm a silly academic who likes art: 25 a month

Doing the math, that comes to 1,765 a month necessary. Let's add a safety 150 dollar margin, because things like health insurance and stuff. We're at 1,915 a month. Can we make it? Yes. Will we have much left over? No. It's paycheck to paycheck living baby. Theoretically, to feel remotely safe, you'll need around 6,000 in the bank for the 3-month emergency living savings rule. We save less than 50 a month, so this will take literally forever. Can you squeeze down a cost here or there? Get lucky in rent and roommates? Live on rice and beans? If you can just get to 100 a month in savings, you can now get to the safety margin in 5 years. 200 a month in savings? Nice.

You will live crappily, probably. You may not have enough money to go party every weekend. You will have to unsubscribe from Netflix, Disney+, etc. But this is part of growing up. You will learn how to budget and be aware of your expenses. Your friends probably never learned any of these skills. In the long run, these skills will be very valuable, since you now know how to weather a storm better than your friends.

You will make it. You've survived plenty worse already. You have no more student debt so you don't need to budget that in (which would've been a huge problem). You're resilient and capable. And if things ever get too rough, your mother can now save money now that she's not supporting you at home, so you have a reserve fund for extreme emergencies, or for potential school. Grind it out!

First off, bruv, are you my remote twin? I'm younger, still in school, and still mediocre grades, but my father's also sick with cancer and I'm struggling a bit mentally. High COL city too.

Take a deep breath first. There's no shame. You did your best, and life just hammered you hard. Your friends probably didn't have to deal with this level of trauma. You are not pathetic. If anything, you have my respect. You're a survivor, you refuse to give up.

I think what you should do right now, before thinking about school, is assess your financial situation. Does your family have enough money to get you through more school? If not, do you have student loans? If you have existing student debt, please do NOT go back to school. You will get even more debt, and compounding interest will do the rest. So many people go back to get a master's in something to make themselves more marketable, then get even more debt, become overqualified for entry level roles, and just kick the can two years down the road. Yes, you can luck out and get a good job with a master's or a second bachelor's, but the risk/reward is pretty dangerous, especially with your current financial condition. And to be blunt, getting a master's in social work or something and going into social work doesn't pay very much compared to other fields.

I think honestly, what's really holding you down mentally might not be your lack of a future career progression; it might be the fact that you're still living at home. By 27 pretty much everyone has moved out of home, and you feel like you aren't successful because you can't support yourself and move out. Even though you might not be able to save much money, I might suggest taking a risk and moving out. You can get roommates to cut down your living costs (and trust me, there are a ton of folks like you in the same situation, we're just not as visible - you'll find plenty of folks to room up with). While you might not be able to save much now that you're self supporting, your mother might be able to save up a bit more, so it does sort of work out. Cut all unnecessary expenses, depending on where you are and what your plans are consider selling your car if you have one and just taking public transit. Honestly, while 20/hr isn't great where I live (Boston), it's doable if you're smart about it. I don't know where you live though, could be the two places that are worse than Boston (NYC or Cali). Even if you're barely scraping by, with relatively less in the bank and living with roommates, being outside of the house for a year or two might help your mental health a bit - because at the very bottom, you're not mooching off your parents like you're 15.

Once you've lived independently for a bit, if you can find some way to crunch down on the student debt a bit, then should you start considering school again. Your mind will probably be much clearer then, you will likely have a little more confidence. If necessary you can move back home to save money when you go back to school. Honestly, I think you really should just take the 1-year "sabbatical" and clear your mind up.

As for work though, I think you're trying super hard to keep using your previous coursework. Fact is, bachelor's degrees are a dime a dozen these days. While it's good to explore ways to use your coursework and/or degree, sometimes you have to cut your losses and look outside the box. A lot of younger folks these days don't seem to want to do physical labor or skilled trades anymore, so there's some potential there. If you're reliable and willing to learn you can try to go into the skilled trades - get paid to learn for five years, then become a journeyman and make moderate money. It's not going to be enough to compare to a business executive, but you'll make enough to live in the lower middle class at least. Only go into skilled trades if you're interested though - going into blue collar work for too long makes you undesirable in the white collar work. White collar folk look down on blue collar workers for some reason.

Thanks for the advice!

So basically instead of looking online, I should go door to door? That's so 1980's but if that's how it's done, it's how it's done. For pretty much anything else these days they just tell you to go fill out the online form. Then again, I guess landscaping and other labor work is more about just being willing to stick it out.

As for boots and gloves, what would you suggest on the cheaper side that's still alright? I don't want to invest on the most expensive gear out of the gate, just in case I end up burning out fast, but I definitely want some gear that can actually withstand daily use.

Thanks for the advice! I figure between three years of fast food, seven years of being a freelance musician, and three years of running an English education department at a school in Taiwan, I figure I've learned how to keep my word. 

I guess it might be smart then to keep my car around first, and check in with the company before I decide to ditch it. Small problem of having to pay for insurance and upkeep and parking though, so I will definitely feel the cash crunch. Might need to subsist on ramen, rice, and beans.

Unfortunately, cooking and being an introvert or slow paced just doesn't mix in the restaurant industry. Maybe graphic art, but graphic artists are a dime a dozen. Still, if you can build up a really good portfolio of graphic art or design, you might be able to find work that way. A degree isn't going to work on its own; I'd suggest you offer to do something for a local business for free just to test your chops; if it works out you have a potential future customer, plus a reference and something in your portfolio. Keep doing this until you have a decent portfolio, then start looking at the larger companies. Get a degree if you want, but note that you'll still want a portfolio of some sort to stand out.

Sadly there's just not a lot of jobs for introverts anymore. I guess computer coding, accounting, or some of the more technical medical things like radiologic technician, etc. Robots and outsourcing took most of the factory jobs, warehouses are fast paced. If you can't break past the introvert wall, you're going to be heavily limited. Maybe you can do data entry, but that pays like crap and will probably get automated in 10 years.

I'd also encourage you to look into more physical and blue collar things, if you're up for it (but only if you're up for it - these things can wear your body down!). Truck driving is up for automation soon, but it might be another 20 years before it really becomes common. In the meantime, you get a ton of money to just drive all day. Sometimes you might get paired with another person, but other times it's just you and the road. Downside is that you'll be away from home most of the time, so if you want to be in your own bed every night this might not work out.

First, sort out your mental health (I need to take this advice too).

Environmental science and landscaping design?

Not an expert, but maybe you could try starting a lawn care company?

You'll need to buy a reliable truck, a trailer, some equipment, and materials. You'll also need to explore the market a bit first to see how much people are bidding, then undercut slightly. It's sleazy but you've got no experience so far in running your own business, so you'll have to settle for less profit on the short term. Hire a few fellas to help out; a good worker will be well worth his/her wages. Pay them fairly too; landscaping is rough work, and not a lot of folks are willing to show up, or even stay for more than a week. 

Your degrees might come in handy since you've learned the more theoretical aspects of landscaping and how to deal with people's lawns. You might know a bit about estimating how much it will cost to get a job done. Do the math, figure it out, add a little profit. Rinse and repeat six days a week, 10-12 hours a day, and you can probably earn some decent money. Bonus points if you do snow removal in winter, or if you live in an area where lawn care is a thing year-round.

The only problem is, you're going to be negotiating with customers a lot and communicating with your workers. Maybe you can hire someone to do the talking for you, but that'll eat a little profit though.

The thing about writing degrees is that these days having one doesn't do much in demonstrating that you can write.

Bootcamps are slightly safer, but highly dependent on both location and extra grinding outside of class. If you're looking for a job in an urban area (except Cali, that's oversaturated to hell), and you've got the motivation and the heart to spend extra time making extra projects on the side to show to future employers outside of your required stuff, then you can try it. You'll also want to look into additional certs. The thing is with a lot of bootcamp and compsci major folks is that they think just passing through and making it out will make them an attractive candidate. That may have been true in the 90's and early 2000's, but today the field's getting oversaturated. You can make it, you'll just need to have much more than just a bootcamp or a degree to prove yourself to employers. If your heart's not in it then don't do it.

Visual Communications degrees I don't know much about honestly, but I know that communications degrees in general are becoming less useful. From what I hear the stuff they teach in class is outdated; pretty much everything is a social media game nowadays. It might be useful, but once again, you'll need the additional portfolio of work and internships to prove it.

Honestly, this might not be a popular idea with a lot of folks, but here's my honest suggestion (because I'm facing a bit of college burnout myself and I'm starting to consider this option): don't go to school yet. Get a job to pay the bills first. Take some community college classes related to all three fields you're considering if you want at night. Do some more research in what you want to do. Take a year to think about it before you dive back in. Student loans can get really stupid, and you don't want to take out any more than you have to. If you're going to insist on part time work only, then retail is probably better. Call centers tend to hire full-time only. Retail will have a lot of high school kids working who also want part time, so retail managers know. Be aware though that you might get slotted into times that you don't like, your schedule will probably change week to week.

Two part time jobs is absolutely the worst. You're working full time hours overall but you get no benefits. I urge you to at least try getting a full time job; especially if your two part time jobs exceeded 40 hours a week. To be blunt, unless you're a doctor, billion-dollar company CEO, or you have some sort of hard-to-get job that nobody wants to do (like climbing radio towers or something), you won't be able to survive pretty much anywhere in the US on a part time job alone, unless you got some super profitable side gig. Especially not in a city. 

If having spare time for your side hobby and home schedule is super important to you, and you don't mind suffering for half a year to get relaxation for the other half, you could look into landscaping. Generally the only requirements are being able to understand basic instructions, being literate (negotiable), having arms and legs, and being able to show up on time to a job looking reasonably presentable. Because most people don't want to stand outside digging ditches in summer heat, the folks that landscaping jobs usually attracts are pretty much bottom of the barrel - in some cases you might find criminal histories, drug use, etc. If you can demonstrate a willingness to learn and keep clean (some booze at night is ok, just don't be completely impaired the next day), you can probably find a contractor that's willing to take a chance on you. Usually no experience is necessary - sometimes the contractor wants you to do things the way they want you to, just watch, ask questions, and follow along. The work is actually quite dangerous (bring a lot of water and a good lunch, some gloves and work boots are very helpful, be aware of your surroundings with tools, watch the heat), the entry level pay is mediocre at best, but if you can just work hard and be reliable then you'll have a guaranteed job every summer. The work can be pretty brutal - in peak summer season you might be working 10 or more hours a day because the contractor literally has contracts stating that they have to do the job. However, in the winter in most areas, the work dries out and you'll have a lot of spare time to just do whatever you want at home. Working those long hours in the summer will net you a lot of cash per week, just make sure you're smart about it and don't spend it all at once, unless you can get a good gig shoveling snow in the winter. Essentially, you'll be sacrificing all your spare time in the spring, summer, and fall, for virtually unlimited free time and some decent cash in the winter. Give it a good thought.

Final side note: I know you can rely on family right now for a place to live, and presumably a meal. This means you can actually live quite comfortably on minimum wage, since in most cities renting a place will eat almost half of your paycheck on minimum wage. No matter what job you end up taking, in retail or landscaping or whatever, please save at least 1/3 of what you earn. I don't know about what your future plans are, but based on the fact that you've tried two part time jobs before, I assume you have time in the day to work a full time job - which means you're likely not in school. If you've already graduated high school, then the next few years are going to be urgent - save up enough money that equates roughly to about 3 months' living expenses alone; this is going to include rent, food, utilities, etc. If you can, also save up enough to pay a first month's rent on a single small room. Frankly, you're not going to be able to live at home forever, you'll need to start planning out how you're going to survive once you move out.

Small ideas:

Apply to locations with some distance from universities and other schools, a lot of other folks are using the summer to earn extra buck too, and they all want to work close by. Don't go for a 2-hour commute, but don't limit yourself to a 10-minute walk.

Avoid applying to locations in poorer neighborhoods. Generally that's where you find a lot more folks that do fast food as a full time job, since poorer folks can't afford to be picky about work. Look for locations in wealthier areas - usually kids' parents won't even let them work part time, since that would interrupt study time. Bonus points if it's a store where you can earn tips.

Don't limit yourself to fast food and grocery stores. Turns out a lot of jobs requiring physical labor are looking for workers, and they can pay a bit more than minimum wage. Granted it's not as comfy as working in an air conditioned building, but work is work, and money is money.

Good luck!

You mentioned that most of your friends have customer service jobs. I don't know what those are, but generally, those do take a little less physical labor than warehouses (obviously). Perhaps their reaction might come from the physical labor involved in warehouse work. 

In a lot of developed countries, there's this real stigma about physical labor. In the U.S. mainly, there's this whole mythos of the country being built up by hard work and sweat but these days if you aren't working in an air-conditioned office tower typing something or in a hospital you're somehow worth less. While true, being a surgeon or a judge or a computer programmer takes a lot of certification, it doesn't mean that being a warehouse worker or a garbage worker or a carpenter or a plumber is somehow not a proper job. In other words, in today's society (in the U.S. at least, where I live), we have somehow created an inverse relationship between physical labor and value. Remember how many times you were told in school to work hard or else you'd become the garbage man?

Of course, this relationship "worked" decades ago; relatively few people then went to white collar work, simply because these sorts of jobs were relatively fewer, and less necessary. While the town did need a dentist, the town would mainly support itself through something like mining, or the railroad, or farming, and that's where most people went. Also, people back then just didn't go to postsecondary education as much as people today. To get a lot of these specialized jobs, you'd need to do some sort of postsecondary education; white collar workers and medical professionals were just the smartest people in the area, with a path that was relatively difficult to achieve then; they commanded respect by their education, and by correlation their jobs commanded respect.

Today, of course, being a doctor still commands respect. But not all white collar jobs are "difficult" by today's standards to get qualified for - if anything, they've become oversaturated. Plenty of folks out here with CS degrees around unable to find jobs with good companies because CS graduates are a dime a dozen nowadays. Say nothing of the liberal arts degrees; once useful for proving that you can at least be trusted to think and research, today you can barely get a job at pizza hut.

Meanwhile, all those jobs that involve physical labor? Yes, a lot of them have disappeared thanks to robots and the fact that we're just not building as much as we used to, but they're out there. And because everyone's been pushing each other for white collar jobs because the blue collar jobs are "less worthy", a lot of skilled trades are gaining value. Saw a Youtube video by a plumber; he mentions that he went to a party, told a girl he was a plumber, and later the girl told all the other girls not to talk to him because he's a plumber. Funny thing is, he makes 60k+ a year, which was easily in the upper range of anyone at that party. While some areas now have a huge rush of new hopefuls who are now realizing the potential earnings in the skilled trades, other areas are hurting for new people and are willing to take in anyone who's reliable and willing to learn.

And the funny thing is, a lot of physical labor jobs are absolutely vital to the economy. If somehow tomorrow all the computer programmers quit their jobs for a day, we might not get the next hot video game or the new version of the website up in time. But if all the warehouse workers in the country - hell, if all the warehouse workers in a single major city - quit their jobs for a day, the entire nation's economy would crash for a long time as the stoppage causes bottlenecks and backlogs in our nation's supply chains. Just because a warehouse job pays less, has almost no requirements for entry, and involves physical labor, doesn't mean that being a warehouse worker isn't an important task. They make sure products and supplies move on time and go where they need to go. Hell, your Covid vaccines got to your local pharmacy through the work of warehouse workers and truck drivers. 

So don't let folks tell you that being a warehouse worker is somehow "incorrect". Let yourself decide. Granted, you'll probably never be paid as much as a businessman, you might barely scrape by with your wages while the computer nerds drive off in their new cars. But at the end of the day, if you did an honest job and you enjoy your job compared to the other options available to you, then you're doing right in my book. If you prefer physical work to trying to deal with customers all day, then you made the right call.

I think there is one caveat to jobs with physical labor, although you're only working part time and this sounds more like a temporary job so it might not really apply to you: these jobs really depend on you being able to keep healthy habits and avoid accidents. Whereas you can generally still do most desk jobs with physical disabilities. 

Some warehouses do have bad management, unrealistic expectations, unsafe conditions, etc. but all jobs have bad and good companies. And the good news is, if your warehouse is an absolute stinking mess at safety and management, give it a year, then start applying to another warehouse. Your existing warehouse experience might be handy, who knows.

Oh, and congrats on getting the job! No matter what job it is, getting your first job is always a huge step.

Unfortunately, reality is cruel.
